definition: A finite, non-empty set of symbols from which strings are built, usually written Σ (capital sigma). A machine's input alphabet is the set of characters its input may contain.
example: For binary strings the alphabet is {0, 1}.

definition: A finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. Its length is the number of symbols, written |s|.
example: "abba" is a string of length 4 over the alphabet {a, b}.

definition: The string with no symbols at all, length 0, written ε (epsilon). In a grammar, a rule A → ε deletes A; in an automaton, an ε-move reads no input.
example: The language { aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0 } contains ε, the case n = 0.

definition: The operation that forms every string made by joining zero or more strings from a set. Σ* is the set of all finite strings over the alphabet Σ, including the empty string.
example: {a, b}* = {ε, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aaa, …}.

definition: A pattern built from the empty language, the empty string and single symbols using union (|), concatenation and the Kleene star (*). Formal regular expressions describe exactly the regular languages. Many practical regex engines add features such as back-references that go beyond this.
example: (ab)* matches ε, ab, abab, ababab, …

definition: A machine model where several moves may be allowed at once; the machine accepts if at least one sequence of choices leads to acceptance. It is a mathematical idea ("guess, then check"), not randomness.
example: A nondeterministic PDA for even palindromes "guesses" where the middle is.

definition: Having at most one possible move in every situation, so the whole run is fixed by the input.
example: A deterministic TM that ever repeats a configuration will repeat it forever.

definition: A string that reads the same forwards and backwards. Even-length palindromes are exactly the strings w wᴿ: a string followed by its reverse.
example: abba and baab are even-length palindromes over {a, b}; abab is not.

definition: wᴿ is the string w written backwards.
example: If w = abb then wᴿ = bba, and w wᴿ = abbbba.

definition: A set of rewrite rules, each replacing a single variable with a string of variables and terminals, plus a start variable. It generates a language: every terminal string reachable from the start. CFGs can describe nesting, such as balanced brackets.
example: S → aSb | ε generates aⁿbⁿ: ε, ab, aabb, …

definition: A language that some context-free grammar generates, equivalently that some (nondeterministic) pushdown automaton recognises. Every regular language is context-free, but not the other way round.
example: aⁿbⁿ is context-free; aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not.

definition: A grammar whose context-restricted rules rewrite a variable inside specified surrounding symbols without shortening the string, apart from a controlled start-to-empty exception in conventions that allow the empty string. These grammars generate strictly more languages than context-free grammars.
example: A context-sensitive grammar can generate aⁿbⁿcⁿ, which no CFG can.

definition: A placeholder symbol in a grammar that must still be rewritten, conventionally a capital letter such as S, E or T. The start variable is the one every derivation begins from.
example: In S → aSb, S is a variable and a, b are terminals.

definition: A real character of the finished string in a grammar: it is never rewritten. The set of terminals is the grammar's alphabet.
example: In E → E + T, the + is a terminal.

definition: One rule of a grammar, written A → w: the variable A may be replaced by the string w. A vertical bar lists alternatives, so S → aSb | ε is two rules.
example: T → T * F is a production rule of the arithmetic grammar.

definition: One application of one grammar rule to a string, written ⇒. A derivation is a sequence of such steps from the start variable to a string of terminals.
example: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aabb is a 3-step derivation.

definition: A partly rewritten string in a derivation: it may still contain variables. The final, all-terminal sentential form is a sentence of the language.
example: aaSbb is a sentential form on the way to aabb.

definition: A derivation that always rewrites the leftmost variable first. Parse trees and leftmost derivations match one-to-one, so counting either counts the other.
example: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ id + T … is leftmost.

definition: A tree showing how a grammar produces a string: each internal node is a variable, its children are the right-hand side of the rule used, and the leaves read left to right spell the string. Its shape encodes grouping such as operator precedence.
example: In id + id * id, the parse tree puts id * id lower, so it is evaluated first.

definition: A grammar in which some string has two or more different parse trees (equivalently, two leftmost derivations). Deciding whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous is undecidable.
example: E → E + E | E * E | id gives id + id * id two trees.

definition: A context-free language for which every context-free grammar is ambiguous, so rewriting within that grammar class cannot remove ambiguity.
example: { aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k } is inherently ambiguous: every grammar for it gives some strings of the form aⁿbⁿcⁿ two parse trees.

definition: The ambiguity in "if a then if b then x else y": the else could belong to either if. C, C++ and Java attach it to the nearest unmatched if.
example: With a false, if (a) if (b) x(); else y(); runs nothing.

definition: The convention for grouping repeated infix operators: left-associative subtraction groups the first two operands, while a right-associative operator groups from the right. In suitable layered expression grammars, left or right recursion encodes the corresponding grouping; arbitrary recursion alone does not guarantee an unambiguous grammar.
example: 8 − 4 − 2 is 2 with left associativity, not 6.

definition: A grammar is left-recursive when a variable can derive a string beginning with that same variable; a direct example is E → E + T. Naive recursive descent may recurse forever on it; LR parsing can handle suitable left-recursive grammars.
example: Rewriting E → E + T | T as a loop "T, then any number of + T" removes it.

definition: A grammar form with rules A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal), optionally allowing S → ε when S never occurs on any right-hand side. Every CFG can be converted to it while preserving its language. In logic, CNF instead means conjunctive normal form.
example: S → AT | AB, T → SB, A → a, B → b is a CNF grammar for aⁿbⁿ (n ≥ 1).

definition: A unit rule rewrites one variable to another single variable (A → B); an ε-rule rewrites a variable to the empty string (A → ε). Conversion to Chomsky normal form removes both (keeping S → ε only if needed).
example: Replacing A → B, B → b with A → b removes a unit rule.

definition: A dynamic-programming parser for grammars in Chomsky normal form. It fills a table of which variables can derive each substring, from short spans to long ones, in O(n³ × |G|) time for an input of length n and grammar size |G|.
example: For "aabb", CYK finds S derives the whole string, so aabb is in the language.

definition: A standard text notation for writing context-free grammars, used in language specifications. Rules look like <expr> ::= <expr> "+" <term>.
example: Early language reports such as ALGOL 60 used BNF.

definition: BNF extended with shorthand for optional parts and repetition, such as [ … ] and { … }. It describes the same languages more compactly.
example: digits = digit { digit } means one or more digits.

definition: A tool that takes a grammar and produces parser code automatically.
example: Yacc, Bison and ANTLR are parser generators.

definition: A classic LALR parser generator from 1970s Unix ("yet another compiler-compiler"). It reports grammar conflicts such as shift/reduce.
example: The dangling else causes a yacc shift/reduce conflict, resolved by shifting.

definition: The GNU parser generator, compatible with yacc. It builds LALR(1) parsers by default and also offers GLR parsing for grammars that need it.
ANother Tool for Language Recognition: a widely used parser generator that builds top-down (LL-style) parsers using adaptive prediction (ALL(*)).

A point where an LR parser cannot tell whether to read the next token (shift) or complete a grammar rule (reduce). It often signals ambiguity; yacc and Bison resolve it by shifting unless told otherwise.
example: For the dangling else, shifting attaches else to the nearest if.

definition: A top-down parser that reads input Left to right and builds a Leftmost derivation, choosing rules by looking k tokens ahead. Recursive-descent parsers are LL-style.
example: An LL(1) parser picks each rule from just the next token.

definition: A bottom-up parser reading input left to right and constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse, using a fixed lookahead bound. For a fixed suitable LR grammar, its deterministic pushdown parsing procedure has a linear input-time bound.
example: Knuth (1965) showed LR(k) grammars describe exactly the deterministic context-free languages.

definition: Look-Ahead LR: a space-saving variant of LR(1) parsing used by yacc and by default in Bison. It handles slightly fewer grammars than full LR(1).
Generalised LR: an LR-style parser that follows several possible parses at once when the grammar has conflicts. It handles any CFG, including ambiguous ones, at a higher worst-case cost.

A top-down parsing technique using procedures for grammar variables. Naive direct recursive descent can recurse indefinitely on left-recursive rules; grammar rewriting or specialised left-recursion handling is needed.
A grammar-like formalism with ordered choice: A / B tries A first and commits if it succeeds. So a PEG never has two parses of the same input. CPython has used a PEG parser since Python 3.9.
A design document proposing a change to Python. PEP 617 replaced CPython's LL(1) parser with a PEG parser.
A technique in C compilers where the lexer consults the symbol table to tell type names (from typedef) apart from ordinary identifiers, because C parsing depends on that context.
example: In a * b; the lexer must know if a is a type.

definition: A compiler data structure recording each declared name (variable, type, function) and its properties. Checks such as "declared before use" are done with it, outside the grammar.
The compiler phase after parsing that checks meaning rather than syntax: declarations, types and scopes. It handles rules a context-free grammar cannot express.
A C keyword that declares a new name for a type. Because of it, whether a * b; is a multiplication or a declaration depends on earlier declarations.
example: typedef int a; makes a * b; declare b as a pointer to int.

definition: The field of getting computers to process human language. Before neural networks, it often used probabilistic CFGs and chart parsing.
A CFG with a probability on each rule, used to pick the most likely parse tree of a sentence.
A family of dynamic-programming parsers (CYK is one) that store reusable partial parsing results in a table, or chart, to avoid redoing work.
A finite automaton plus an unbounded stack it can read and change only at the top. Nondeterministic PDAs recognise exactly the context-free languages.
example: A PDA checks aⁿbⁿ by pushing an A per a and popping one per b.

definition: A pushdown automaton with at most one enabled move in each configuration, with no competition between an enabled epsilon move and an input-consuming move. Deterministic PDAs recognise the deterministic context-free languages, a strict subclass of the context-free languages.
example: A DPDA can check w c wᴿ (centre marked) but not w wᴿ.

definition: A language recognised by a deterministic pushdown automaton. Under standard end-of-input conventions these are exactly the languages admitting LR(k) grammars; this does not mean every grammar for such a language is accepted by every practical parser generator.
example: Balanced brackets form a DCFL; even palindromes do not.

definition: A last-in, first-out store: you can push an item onto the top, pop the top item off, or look at the top, but nothing deeper. A PDA's stack alphabet (Γ, gamma) is the set of symbols it may push.
example: Push A, push B, pop: you get B back, and A is now on top.

definition: The two stack operations: push puts a symbol on top; pop removes the top symbol.
A special symbol, often $, placed first on a PDA's stack so the machine can tell when the stack is otherwise empty.
example: The aⁿbⁿ PDA accepts when it sees $ on top again after the last b.

definition: A move that reads no input symbol. In a PDA it may still pop or push, so a machine can make many ε-moves, even infinitely many, without consuming input.
example: The palindrome PDA uses an ε-move to jump from pushing to popping.

definition: The rule book of an automaton, written δ (delta): given the current state and what is read, it gives the next move. For a TM, δ(q, a) = (r, b, D): go to state r, write b, move in direction D.
example: δ(C, 1) = (C, 0, L) is the carry rule of the binary increment machine.

definition: In a Turing machine, the accept state and the reject state are the halting states: entering either stops the run with yes or no, and they have no outgoing rules. Every other state is a working state; busy-beaver counts give the number of working states only.
example: The 2-state busy beaver has working states A and B plus a separate halt state.

definition: A complete snapshot of a running machine: its state plus everything in memory. For a PDA that is state, input position and stack; for a TM, state, tape contents and head position.
example: 1 0 q 1 1 means tape 1011, state q, head on the third symbol.

definition: Joining strings end to end, written by putting them side by side. For languages, L₁L₂ is every string made of one from L₁ followed by one from L₂.
example: Concatenating ab and ba gives abba.

definition: A property every context-free language has: every long enough string s splits as uvxyz, with v and y not both empty and |vxy| at most the CFL pumping length p, so that uvⁱxyⁱz stays in the language for every i ≥ 0. Showing a language lacks it proves it is not context-free.
example: aⁿbⁿcⁿ fails it, so it is not context-free.

definition: The number p in the context-free pumping lemma: every string in the language at least p characters long can be split as uvxyz and pumped. It depends only on the language; for a grammar in Chomsky normal form with k variables, p = 2^k works.
example: For { aⁿbⁿ }, p = 2 works: in aabb take v = a and y = b next to each other in the middle.

definition: A stronger form of the context-free pumping lemma (Ogden, 1968) that lets you mark which positions must be pumped. It proves some results, such as inherent ambiguity, that the plain lemma cannot.

Turing's 1936 model of computation: a finite control (states) plus an unbounded tape of cells, with a head that reads, writes and moves one cell left or right per step. On each input it accepts, rejects or runs forever. Formally a 7-tuple (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, q_accept, q_reject).
example: A TM decides aⁿbⁿcⁿ by crossing off one a, one b and one c per pass.

definition: A TM's memory: an unbounded row of cells, each holding one symbol. The input starts on it and every other cell holds the blank. A run that halts only ever touches finitely many cells.
The part of a Turing machine that points at one tape cell: it reads that cell, writes a symbol there and moves one cell left (L) or right (R) each step.
The fixed, finite set of states that tells a machine what to do next, separate from its unbounded memory (tape or stack).
Γ (gamma): every symbol a TM may write, including the input alphabet Σ, the blank (often _) and extra markers such as X.
example: For the aⁿbⁿcⁿ machine, Γ = {a, b, c, X, Y, Z, _}.

definition: A TM with several tapes and heads. It recognises the same languages as a single-tape TM. For a run at least as long as the input, the standard single-tape simulation has a quadratic bound in the multi-tape step count.

A TM that may have several possible moves at each step; it accepts if any branch accepts. Deterministic TMs recognise the same languages by searching all branches breadth-first, possibly exponentially more slowly.
A TM technique of overwriting already-matched symbols with markers (such as X, Y, Z) so later passes can skip them.
example: Each pass marks one a as X, one b as Y and one c as Z.

definition: The convention that a TM with no rule for its current state and symbol rejects at once, so rejecting transitions need not be written out.
For a machine or program: never halt on that input. A TM's three possible outcomes are accept, reject and loop forever, and the third is the root of undecidability.
example: while True: pass runs forever.

definition: For the standard two-symbol model on a two-way tape, S(n) is the greatest blank-tape runtime among halting machines with n working states; Σ(n) is the greatest number of ones left by such a machine. Both functions are uncomputable and eventually exceed every total computable function of n.
An online collaboration that in 2024 proved S(5) = 47,176,870, with the proof checked in the Coq/Rocq proof assistant.

A TM recognises a language L if it accepts exactly the strings in L; on other strings it may reject or loop. A language with a recogniser is Turing-recognisable, also called recursively enumerable (RE).
example: A_TM is recognisable: simulate M on w and accept if it does.

definition: A Turing machine that halts on every input, accepting or rejecting. A decider for L accepts the strings in L and rejects all others.
example: The crossing-off machine is a decider for aⁿbⁿcⁿ.

definition: A language (yes/no problem) that some Turing machine decides: it always halts with the right answer. Also called recursive. Decidable means an algorithm exists for all inputs, not that it is fast.
example: "Does this DFA accept w?" is decidable.

definition: A language is co-recognisable if its complement is Turing-recognisable. A language is decidable exactly when it is both recognisable and co-recognisable.
example: The complement of A_TM is co-recognisable but not recognisable.

definition: Running several possibly endless computations together by alternating single steps, so any one that halts is eventually noticed.
example: Alternate a recogniser for L and one for its complement; one must accept.

definition: The claim that every function computable by an effective procedure (a finite, mechanical method needing no insight) is computable by a Turing machine. It is a thesis, not a theorem, because "effective procedure" is informal.
example: It lets you read "no TM decides X" as "no algorithm decides X".

definition: The stronger, physical claim that anything a physical device can compute is Turing-computable. Proposed hypercomputers would contradict it but appear to need unrealistic resources.

The claim that any reasonable model of computation can be simulated by a (probabilistic) Turing machine with at most polynomial slowdown. Quantum computing, via Shor's algorithm, casts doubt on it, though it is not disproved.
A finite list of exact, mechanical instructions that always gives its result in finitely many steps when followed, needing no insight or ingenuity. It is the informal idea of an algorithm.
example: Long multiplication by hand is an effective procedure.

definition: A partial computable function is calculated by a Turing machine that halts with its value whenever that value is defined, and diverges on inputs outside its domain. A total computable function is defined on every input and its computing machine therefore always halts.
example: Addition is computable; the busy beaver function is not.

definition: Alonzo Church's 1936 model of computation with only variables, function definition (λx. body) and function application. It computes exactly the same functions as Turing machines and underlies functional programming.
example: Applying the identity function λx. x to an argument y gives y: (λx. x) y reduces to y.

definition: A way to encode the number n in λ-calculus as the function "apply f n times": λf. λx. f(f(…f(x)…)).
example: The numeral for 2 is λf. λx. f(f(x)).

definition: A lambda-calculus term that provides recursion by turning a function into a fixed point of itself. The usual Y construction works with non-strict evaluation; an eager-language construction such as Z delays recursive calls so its initial unfolding can work in Python.
Evaluating a function’s arguments before calling it, as Python does. Delayed evaluation postpones work; lazy evaluation evaluates it only when needed and usually shares the result.

A definition of computable functions on whole numbers, built from simple functions by composition, recursion and unbounded search (μ). Developed by Gödel, Herbrand and Kleene, it is equivalent to Turing machines.

An abstract machine with finitely many instructions that manipulate registers holding unbounded natural numbers. Counter-machine variants use increment, decrement and zero tests; suitable two-counter machines are universal. Random-access variants also allow indexed memory access and require explicit operation-cost assumptions when comparing efficiency.
Emil Post's string-rewriting model: repeatedly delete symbols from the front of a word and append a string chosen by the first deleted symbol. Suitable tag systems are Turing complete.
A grid of cells, each in one of finitely many states, all updated together by the same local rule based on their neighbours.
example: Conway's Game of Life and Rule 110 are cellular automata.

definition: A one-dimensional cellular automaton with two cell states, proved Turing complete by Matthew Cook (published 2004) given suitable repeating background patterns.
John Conway's 1970 two-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell lives or dies based on its 8 neighbours. Patterns such as gliders can be assembled into a universal computer.
An imaginary black box that instantly answers any question of a fixed kind, such as "does this program halt?". Oracle machines are used to compare problems' difficulty, not as real computers.
example: With a halting oracle you could settle Goldbach's conjecture.

definition: A proposed machine that could compute things no Turing machine can, for example by doing infinitely many steps in finite time. None is known to be physically buildable.
A single fixed TM, U, that takes the encoding ⟨M⟩ of any TM M plus an input w and simulates M on w. It is the theoretical basis of interpreters and stored-program computers.
example: CPython running a .py file plays the role of U.

definition: Angle brackets mean "the encoding of": ⟨M⟩ is Turing machine M's rule table written out as a string, and ⟨M, w⟩ encodes M together with an input w. Encodings let machines take other machines as input.
A system is Turing complete if, given unbounded memory and time, it can simulate any Turing machine. It says what is possible, not what is fast or practical.
example: Python, C++ templates and Rule 110 are Turing complete; formal regular expressions are not.

definition: A minimalist esoteric programming language with eight one-character instructions operating on a tape of byte cells. With an unbounded tape it is Turing complete.
C++'s compile-time generic programming feature. Template instantiation can express universal computation if compiler limits are ignored.

x86 is the instruction-set family of most PCs; mov is its data-move instruction. Stephen Dolan showed in 2013 that mov instructions alone, plus one jump back to the start, can simulate a TM, assuming unbounded memory.
A collectible card game. Churchill, Biderman and Herrick showed in 2019 that a combination of its cards can simulate a universal Turing machine.

A system for running small sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel. A verifier only accepts programs it can show are safe and terminating, including bounded loops, so eBPF is deliberately not Turing complete.
The small stack-based language that Bitcoin transactions use to state spending conditions. It has no loops, so every script finishes.
A Python-like configuration language used by build systems such as Bazel. Its core forbids recursion and unbounded loops so evaluation terminates.
A programmable configuration language designed to be total: every Dhall program terminates.

A dependently typed functional language and proof assistant. Its normal termination checker requires a justification of termination for recursive definitions; guarded coinduction and explicitly disabled checks need separate treatment.

A proof assistant renamed Rocq in 2025, used to write and mechanically check proofs. Its ordinary recursive definitions require a termination argument; coinductive definitions instead have guarded productivity conditions, and explicit options can disable checks at the cost of logical guarantees.
example: The 2024 proof of S(5) was checked in Coq.

definition: An interactive proof assistant for machine-checked proofs, often used with higher-order logic.
Software in which a human writes proofs that the computer checks step by step. It gives strong guarantees but needs human guidance.
example: Coq/Rocq, Agda and Isabelle are proof assistants.

definition: Programming in a language where every program must terminate. It gives strong guarantees but cannot express every computation, so it is not Turing complete.
A way of defining and reasoning about possibly infinite structures, such as endless streams, in proof assistants while keeping each step productive.
A blockchain platform that runs programs called smart contracts on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM).
The stack-based virtual machine that executes Ethereum smart-contract code. Every transaction has a finite gas budget, so execution always stops.

A signed instruction submitted to Ethereum that can transfer funds or execute contract code. A transaction executing code has a finite gas limit; its execution can finish successfully, fail, or exhaust its gas, but cannot continue indefinitely under EVM rules.

Ethereum's unit of execution cost. Each transaction pays for a finite amount; continuing computation uses it up, so execution stops normally, with an error, or out of gas. Some terminating opcodes such as STOP cost zero.
The part of a machine or virtual-machine instruction that says which operation to perform.
example: STOP is an EVM opcode.

definition: A purely functional, lazily evaluated programming language rooted in the λ-calculus.
A functional programming language in the ML family, with static type inference.
One of the oldest programming languages (1958), built on lists and heavily influenced by the λ-calculus.
The virtual machine that runs Java bytecode, acting as an interpreter and just-in-time compiler.
A binary unit of data: 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824 bytes. A GB (gigabyte) is the decimal 10⁹ bytes.
example: 16 GiB = 16 × 2³⁰ × 8 = 2³⁷ bits.

definition: A computer using qubits and quantum gates. Under the standard model with effectively specified gates, quantum computation does not extend what is computable by classical machines, but may change efficiency; unbounded-resource claims idealise hardware limits away.

The basic operation of the quantum circuit model: a fixed reversible (unitary) transformation of one or a few qubits, playing the role a logic gate plays in a classical circuit. A quantum computation is a sequence of such gates followed by measurement.
example: The Hadamard gate turns a qubit in state 0 into an equal superposition of 0 and 1.

definition: A finite sequence of quantum gates acting on qubits, with measurement used to obtain classical outcomes. The standard circuit model describes quantum computation using these operations rather than a particular hardware device.
Bounded-error quantum polynomial time: the decision problems a quantum computer solves in polynomial time with error probability at most 1/3.
example: Factoring (as a decision problem) is in BQP.

definition: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time: the decision problems a randomised classical algorithm solves in polynomial time with error probability at most 1/3.
The decision problems a deterministic Turing machine solves in polynomial time. Single-tape and multi-tape TMs give the same class P.
The language of all encodings ⟨M, w⟩ where Turing machine M accepts input w. It is recognisable (simulate M) but undecidable, and its complement Ā_TM is not even recognisable.
The halting problem written as a language: all ⟨M, w⟩ where M halts on w. HALT_ε is the special case of a blank input. Both are recognisable but undecidable.
The set of Turing machines (encoded) that accept no string at all. It is undecidable and co-recognisable but not recognisable.
The set of pairs of Turing machines that accept exactly the same language. Neither it nor its complement is recognisable.
The language D built in Cantor's argument: it contains the i-th string exactly when the i-th listed language does not, so it differs from every language in the list.

A way of turning any question about problem A into a question about problem B, so a solver for B would give a solver for A. It shows A is no harder than B; to prove B undecidable, reduce a known undecidable problem to B.
example: Reducing A_TM to HALT_TM shows the halting problem is undecidable.

definition: A ≤ₘ B means a total computable function f exists with x ∈ A exactly when f(x) ∈ B, for every input x. Decidability and recognisability both carry backwards along it.
example: f(⟨M, w⟩) = ⟨M′, w⟩, where M′ loops instead of rejecting, shows A_TM ≤ₘ HALT_TM.

definition: A is Turing reducible to B if A can be decided by a machine that may ask a B-oracle any number of questions and post-process the answers. It is more general than a many-one reduction.
example: Every language is Turing reducible to its complement: ask the oracle and negate.

definition: Henry Rice's 1953 result: every non-trivial semantic property of Turing machines (one that depends only on the recognised language and holds for some but not all machines) is undecidable.
example: "Is L(M) empty?" and "does M accept hello?" are undecidable by Rice.

definition: A property of programs or machines that depends only on what they compute or accept, not on how they are written. Two machines with the same language either both have it or both lack it.
example: "Accepts at least one string" is semantic; "has 5 states" is not.

definition: A property that some machines have and some do not. A trivial property is true of all machines or of none, and is trivially decidable.
example: "L(M) is recognisable" is trivial: every TM has it.

definition: A property of a program's text or a machine's description, such as its number of states, rather than of its behaviour. Rice's theorem does not apply to these.
example: "Does the source contain eval?" is syntactic and decidable.

definition: The sequence of configurations a machine passes through on an input. Encoding accepting histories as strings is a key trick for proving grammar problems undecidable.
Given dominoes each with a top and bottom string, is there a non-empty sequence (repeats allowed) whose top and bottom strings spell the same thing? Emil Post proved it undecidable in 1946.
Does a polynomial equation with integer coefficients have an integer solution? Matiyasevich (1970), building on Davis, Putnam and Robinson, proved no algorithm can decide it.
example: x² + y² = 3 has no integer solution; x² + y² = 5 does (x = 1, y = 2).

definition: The Matiyasevich–Robinson–Davis–Putnam theorem: every recursively enumerable set of natural-number tuples is Diophantine, meaning membership is equivalent to existence of auxiliary natural numbers satisfying a polynomial equation with integer coefficients. It implies the undecidability of Hilbert’s tenth problem.

The polymorphic λ-calculus (Girard, Reynolds). In Church style terms carry type annotations and checking is decidable; in Curry style they do not, and Wells (1994) proved typability and type checking undecidable.

Typability asks whether a term has any type; type checking asks whether it has a specified type. Type inference tries to obtain a type from the term, with guarantees and decidability depending on the type system.
example: Java's checker rejects int x = flag ? 1 : "a"; under its typing rules.

definition: A framework (Cousot and Cousot, 1977) for sound static analysis: run the program over simplified abstract values, such as signs or ranges, that safely over-approximate every real run.
example: Tracking only "positive / zero / negative" can prove a divisor is never zero.

definition: For an analyser that reports possible bugs, sound over-approximation means it misses no real bug within its stated model, though it can raise false alarms. An unsound bug finder may miss bugs; that alone does not guarantee fewer false alarms. For an undecidable property, no analyser is sound, complete and always terminating on every arbitrary input.
example: An analyser may report possible division by zero for an unknown denominator even when a particular run supplies a nonzero value.

definition: Static application security testing: analysing program code or related representations for potential security bugs without executing the application on concrete inputs. Tools differ in their guarantees and trade-offs; the label alone does not establish soundness.
The C Bounded Model Checker: it checks C programs for errors by exploring all executions up to a fixed bound on loop iterations.

Automatically checking whether a model of a system satisfies a specified property, often by exploring reachable states. Bounded model checking searches for counterexamples only within a chosen bound; absence of one does not alone establish the unbounded property.
example: CBMC checks C programs with loops unrolled up to a chosen bound.

definition: A sound static analyser based on abstract interpretation that proves the absence of runtime errors in embedded C code, used for example on Airbus flight software.
A tool that tries to prove a program always halts. It is conservative: it accepts some terminating programs and rejects or gives up on others, because termination is undecidable.

A compiler optimisation that removes code that can never run or whose result is never used. Because deciding whether a piece of code can ever run is undecidable in general, compilers remove only code they can prove dead.
Whether some execution of a program can reach a given point or event, such as a crash or a print. For Turing-complete models it is undecidable in general.
Using a pointer or reference that points to nothing (null) as if it pointed to real data; usually a crash.
A cap on how long a job may run before it is killed (a timeout). It bounds resources but does not decide halting: a job that hit the limit might have finished later.
example: A build job killed after 60 minutes may just have been slow.

definition: A real cap on memory, execution time, recursion depth or similar resources, imposed by hardware or software. Turing-completeness claims about practical languages idealise appropriate limits away.
example: CPython exposes its interpreter recursion limit through sys.getrecursionlimit(); the limit is finite and configurable.

definition: Code run on demand by a cloud provider without you managing servers, typically with a hard maximum run time.

The unproved conjecture, originating in correspondence in 1742, that every even integer greater than two is a sum of two primes. Published exhaustive computation has verified the even cases through four quintillion; any finite bound leaves the universal conjecture unproved.

A theorem that for any effective transformation of program descriptions there is a program whose computed behaviour equals that of its transformed description. It formalises effective self-reference without requiring a program to read its source file.
A program or statement that refers to itself, such as a machine run on its own description. It is the engine of the diagonal proofs of undecidability.
A formal system is consistent if it cannot prove a contradiction. For a system with effectively checkable proofs, a program can search all proofs and halt if it finds a contradiction.
Repeating a depth-limited depth-first search with limits 1, 2, 3, …, so every finite depth is eventually explored while using little memory.
The most children any node of a search or computation tree has: for a nondeterministic TM, the most moves it can choose from at one step.
example: With branching factor 2, depth 5 has at most 2⁵ = 32 leaves.

definition: The tree of all possible runs of a nondeterministic machine on one input: each node is a configuration, and its children are the configurations one move later.

A computer that stores program instructions in memory rather than fixing the program solely in wiring. A shared instruction-and-data memory is the von Neumann form; stored-program machines can also use separate memories. Programs represented as data can be loaded, inspected and generated.
A widely used open-source operating-system kernel.
The core software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, such as Linux, Windows or macOS.
The Extensible Markup Language: a text format of nested tags for structured data. Its nesting is a context-free feature.
example: nests b inside a.

definition: A low-level, compiled systems programming language from 1972, used for operating systems and embedded code.
The finite set of symbols a pushdown automaton may put on its stack, conventionally named gamma. It can include a bottom marker and symbols that differ from the input alphabet.
A Turing-machine state in which a transition can perform another computation step, rather than stop the machine. Busy-beaver conventions count these working states separately from the halting state.

The tape symbol marking a cell that holds no input or other written data, shown as an underscore in this module. It belongs to the tape alphabet but not the input alphabet; initially every cell outside the input holds it.
